expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation to close the same-role gap on a dated, budgeted plan much faster than five years, and not to keep it quiet.
expectations.evidence: Opens: 'Fix the 6% gap for people in the same role and grade within about six months, tell the works councils now ... A quiet five-year catch-up is more expensive than it looks, and it probably can't stay quiet.' Budgeted: 'Budget it as a one-off correction, not as a rolling five-year line'; 'a dated plan, a budget you've seen, spread across two quarters if cash flow needs it'.

expectations.text: The reply states correctly that equal pay for equal work is already law (Article 157 TFEU or national equal pay law), so a same-role gap is a legal exposure now, whatever the transposition date of the new directive.
expectations.evidence: 'Equal pay for equal work is already law across the EU (Article 157 TFEU), whatever the transposition date.' Also: 'Dutch claims reach back five years (article 3:308 BW)'.

expectations.text: The reply gets the EU Pay Transparency Directive right: a gap of 5% or more within a category of workers that can't be justified by objective, gender-neutral factors and isn't fixed within six months triggers a joint pay assessment with workers' representatives; and it notes at least one of the reporting thresholds and dates, the employee right to information, or that transposition is late (the Dutch law is expected in 2027).
expectations.evidence: 'That applies when a gap of 5% or more in a category of workers can't be justified by objective, gender-neutral factors and isn't fixed within six months.' Plus: 'Dutch reporting should start in June 2028, on 2027 data, for your 420-person entity. Belgian dates aren't set, because the law isn't published. Each legal entity reports for itself' and the employee right to ask for pay levels by sex.

expectations.text: The reply separates the overall gap from the same-role gap and explains how to analyse what objective factors explain, with care for small groups.
expectations.evidence: 'Give the 14% its own plan. Most of it probably comes from who sits in which job and grade.' Analysis: 'Check what explains it: grade, location, tenure, billing level, starting salary. Keep only factors that are objective and gender-neutral. Show the number of people in each cell, and report groups under five only in aggregate. Have counsel review it.' Also asks whether controls could 'be a proxy for gender'.

expectations.text: The reply puts a number on the cost of closing the same-role gap, or shows how to compute it from the payroll data, and frames it for the CFO against the cost of claims, attrition or reputation.
expectations.evidence: Method from payroll: 'the cost of lifting each underpaid person to the level of comparable peers. It will almost certainly be a small fraction of 6% of payroll.' Framed: 'The five-year plan doesn't save that money. It defers it and adds back-pay claims, interest, attrition and a legal position we'd have to defend.' No worked figure, but the computation and framing are clear.

expectations.text: The reply includes telling employees or their representatives honestly and fixing the causes (such as starting pay, promotion or bonus decisions).
expectations.evidence: 'Brief both works councils now (month 1)'; 'Tell people. Say what you found and what you're doing. Say plainly that the gap comes from past pay decisions that leadership owns'; 'Fix the causes (months 2 to 9). Starting salaries negotiated case by case, bonus and promotion decisions without criteria, and penalties for part-time or leave.'

overall_quality.evidence: The most accurate and complete advice: a six-month fix, the Belgian 2012 law and the Dutch consent rights that make silence impossible, five-year back pay, entity-level reporting and a CFO script that offers real control over timing; it lacks only a worked cost figure.

factual_errors.evidence: Checked: Article 157 TFEU, joint pay assessment trigger, Dutch first report June 2028 on 2027, per-entity reporting, Belgian 2012 law (50+ workers, biennial analysis), Belgian works council from 100 workers, 3:308 BW five-year limitation, 27(1)(c) WOR, Belgian law unpublished (fact sheet, Sept 2026). Minor looseness only: 'Any employee can also ask for pay levels' is in the present tense, though the right isn't in force yet; the same reply says 'will soon be able to ask'.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon.

owns_result.evidence: 'Say plainly that the gap comes from past pay decisions that leadership owns, not from anything the underpaid did.'

best_insight.value: It reframes the CFO's 'saving' as pay withheld that women can reclaim for five years under 3:308 BW, so the slow plan defers the cost rather than saving it, and it says to compare routes as 'what we pay plus what the underpaid go without'.
best_insight.evidence: 'Waiting isn't free' bullet and CFO script.

suggestions.assertion: The reply opens with a recommendation to close the same-role gap on a dated, budgeted plan much faster than five years, and not to keep it quiet.
suggestions.reason: 'Much faster than five years' is ambiguous: a two-to-three-year spread (sample A) reads as faster but leaves women knowingly underpaid past the first Dutch report (7 June 2028) and its six-month remedy window. Name a bar, e.g. 'within about a year, before the first report'.

suggestions.assertion: The reply puts a number on the cost of closing the same-role gap, or shows how to compute it from the payroll data, and frames it for the CFO against the cost of claims, attrition or reputation.
suggestions.reason: A bare formula ('6% of the women's pay', 'lift each underpaid person to peers') passes as easily as a worked estimate. If the CFO conversation is the point, ask for an order-of-magnitude figure (about 1 to 1.5% of payroll) or a worked illustration.

suggestions.assertion: The reply includes telling employees or their representatives honestly and fixing the causes (such as starting pay, promotion or bonus decisions).
suggestions.reason: All four samples pass this easily; it doesn't discriminate. Consider checking that the remedy raises the underpaid without freezing others or asking for waivers, and that leadership owns the cause in what staff hear.

No assertion checks the Belgian side, although it is the strongest answer to 'keep it internal': the 2012 pay gap law already requires a biennial pay analysis by sex for the works council. Samples B and C use it; A only points to counsel; D misses it.
No assertion checks that reporting thresholds are applied per legal employer (NL 420, BE 230), not to the combined 650. Sample A got this wrong; B got it right.

eval_feedback.overall: Assertions 2 to 4 discriminate well; 1 needs a clearer speed bar, 5 and 6 are easy to pass, and the Belgian 2012 law and entity-level reporting go unchecked.
